#4210. Every Brand Selling Hybrid Vehicles in the U.S. for 2027

Hybrid car sales are at a high, and that means plenty of choices in segments including SUVs, sedans, vans, and sports cars.

For all the talk about electric vehicles over the past several years, the bigger story is the current hybrid wave. From 2024 until the end of September 2026, gas-electric hybrids soared from just over eight percent of new light-duty vehicle sales to 16 percent, or double the share of EVs, according to the Energy Information Administration. After consecutive years of parallel growth that saw battery-electric and gas-electric vehicles rise together starting in 2020, hybrid sales have never been higher while EVs, despite a spurt in 2025 and 2026, are not recovering.

This means that there’s now more choice than ever among hybrid vehicles: nearly every major automaker offers at least one hybrid model, and many of them offer a wide range of hybrids in various body styles from SUVs to sports cars and everything in between. Here’s a guide to all hybrids on sale, across all segments (excluding 48-volt hybrids that are not designed to power a vehicle solely with electric motors).

Every Brand Selling Sports Cars | Every Brand Selling EVs | Best-Looking Cars

Bentley makes the world’s only four-seat plug-in hybrid convertible, the Continental GTC. The ravishing powertrain, standard with 671 horsepower or 771 horsepower in the Speed and Mulliner, isn’t exclusive to the the Continental range, either. The twin-turbo V-8 and its 22-kWh battery pack are shared with the Flying Spur sedan, both of which claim 30 miles of electric range (we did 49 in the Continental). A turbo V-6 and an 18-kWh battery are found in the Bentayga Hybrid SUV.

BMW offers a sextet of plug-in hybrids that throw heavy punches under hard acceleration. The 550e, 750e, and X5 xDrive50e share a 483-hp setup with a turbo inline-six good for between 34 and 44 miles of electric range, while the M5, M5 Touring and XM electrify a twin-turbo V-8 for a total of 717 or 738 horsepower. We expect to see more hybrid setups on the high-performance end of the lineup in the future, although the next-gen M3 is also offering a fully electric variant, signifying a possible shift in BMW’s strategy.

Chevrolet’s sole hybrids are found within the Corvette lineup. The first is the Grand Sport X, which supplements the base Stingray’s 6.7-liter V-8 with a front electric motor for a total of 721 horsepower. The other is the ZR1X, which costs a quarter-million dollars and pumps 1250 horsepower from a turbo 5.5-liter V-8 and a front electric motor. It gets 12 mpg in the city and goes 225 mph. It’s beyond magnificent. Still, Chevy is planning more mainstream hybrids, as the three-row Traverse SUV is poised to get a hybrid variant in the future.

All mid-engine Ferraris come as hybrids—and 869 horsepower is the bare minimum. That’s the output from the twin-turbo flat-plane V-6 and axial-flux motor in the new 296 Speciale. The wedgy 849 Testarossa stuffs a twin-turbo V-8 and triple motors for 1036 horsepower. For $3.7 million, the almighty F80 goes backward in cylinder count (but with a more powerful twin-turbo V-6 and three motors) and forward with F1 tech for 1184 horsepower. Buy a front-engine Ferrari and you’ll have to settle for nonhybrid V-12s and V-8s.

Ford sold some of the industry’s first PHEVs in the 2010s—remember the Fusion Energi?—but no longer offers any hybrid sedans or SUVs. The Escape Hybrid and PHEV are gone. But one of our favorite hybrids on sale is the Maverick compact pickup, which can hit 40-plus mpg in the city with front- or all-wheel drive. The F-150 PowerBoost, which uses a twin-turbo V-6 with an electric motor, is more capable but not as smooth to drive as the Maverick.

The first Genesis hybrids aren’t launching until the 2028 model year in the U.S., but we decided to include them here anyway. The lineup includes the gorgeous G80 mid-size luxury sedan and the stately GV80 mid-size luxury SUV. Their hybrid powertrains both use turbo 2.5-liter inline-fours and represent the next stage of the Hyundai group’s hybrid expertise. The batteries now use liquid instead of air cooling, a seven-speed automatic replaces the six-speed, and the torque output (391 lb-ft) matches the twin-turbo V-6 in the 3.5T trims.

Honda has been into hybrids almost as long as Toyota has (see the 1999 Honda Insight), and the company’s current hybrid powertrain is a gem. With direct drive (no transmission), the two-motor, 2.0-liter inline-four setup is quick, efficient, and downright fun. It’s available on the CR-V, the Civic sedan and hatchback, and the Accord sedan, and it’s the only choice on the Prelude coupe.

While the Elantra Hybrid takes a hiatus until 2028, Hyundai’s next-best mileage champ is the Sonata Hybrid, which can surpass 50 mpg and offers generous rear leg room. Hyundai’s three compact and mid-size SUVs, including a new-gen Tucson, get hybrid versions and all offer all-wheel drive. Unlike many mainstream hybrids, Hyundai employs a six-speed automatic instead of a CVT or direct drive. The Tucson plug-in hybrid is no longer available.

While Jeep axed the plug-in hybrid 4xe trims of the Wrangler and Grand Cherokee, an extended-range series hybrid is coming to the Grand Wagoneer with a whopping 647 horsepower. The hybrid-only Cherokee compact SUV comes with only 210 horsepower but up to an estimated 39 mpg city rating.

Like Hyundai, Kia’s diversity of gas, hybrid, and electric powertrains has paid off in spades in terms of sales. There are eight hybrids total in the Kia lineup, with plug-in hybrids available on the Sorento and Sportage (no longer on the Niro). Every SUV has a hybrid option, and so does the Carnival minivan.

Surprised to see Lamborghini peddling hybrids? The brand’s lineup is now entirely hybrid, actually, starting with the plug-in hybrid Urus SUV which comes in 789-hp SE and 801-hp Performante versions. Those SUVs can do an estimated 35 miles on electricity. The 907-hp Temerario is also a plug-in hybrid, offering a pitiful four miles of electric range. But the only hybrid that revs to 10,000 rpm. Then there’s the 1001-hp Revuelto and 1050-hp Revuelto SV which pair a giant V-12 with three electric motors. What a time to be alive.

Leave it to Lexus to combine big power with efficiency. This was the brand that in 2008 gave us the LS600hL, a hybrid flagship that could match the refinement from 12-cylinder German sedans. Now that we live in an SUV world, the LX700h is the modern equivalent—at up to $143,000, it’s the rare four-passenger hybrid SUV with four-wheel drive and a fully reclining rear seat. The TX500h is the next step down (the PHEV is gone for 2027). The RX and NX each offer three hybrid trims including plug-ins, while the new ES350h is now the sole hybrid sedan.

Lincoln moved away from hybrids only to come running back—and they took a long way home. The brand’s two hybrid SUVs, the compact Corsair and mid-size two-row Nautilus, are plucked straight from China, since Ford hasn’t yet carved out factory space for these models in North America. They enjoy a substantial exterior refresh for 2027, too. Each comes with turbo inline-fours and all-wheel drive, while the Nautilus goes screen crazy with a 48-inch display hugging the bottom of the windshield.

While the CX-50 Hybrid uses a Toyota-based powertrain, the CX-90 Hybrid is all Mazda. It’s a nicely styled three-row plug-in hybrid SUV with an estimated 25 miles of electric range. The two-row CX-70 Hybrid is discontinued, but there’s a CX-5 Hybrid on the horizon, though it may not arrive until 2028.

Want a Le Mans racer as a comfortable supercar? There’s no better choice than a McLaren Artura, which has a howling twin-turbo V-6 that has the party trick of leaving and arriving in complete silence. With 11 miles of estimated electric range, it can go nearly three times as far on a charge than a Lamborghini Temerario can. The combined 690 horsepower and McLaren’s light-as-a-feather chassis are heavenly. Choose the coupe or a spider.

While AMG customers weren’t so enthusiastic about the C63 and its F1-derived four-cylinder plug-in hybrid powertrain, they’re happy plugging into turbo-sixes and turbo V-8s on the higher-end models. Every hybrid AMG is PHEV, whether it’s a sedan, wagon, SUV, convertible, or coupe. The E Performance trims of the SL and GT Coupe make more than 1000 pound-feet of torque.

Mercedes-Benz’s three hybrid models are all plug-in hybrids just like their AMG cousins, only less potent. The S580e is our personal favorite, as we were able to reach 58 miles of all-electric range on the highway, handily beating the factory estimate. The GLE500e also shares the same inline-six and delivers similar range, while the GLC350e has an inline-four. Like the AMGs, the GLE and S-class hybrids support DC fast charging, a rare feature on a PHEV.

Mitsubishi was first to market with a plug-in SUV, and it hasn’t really received due credit. Part of it is the premium price the Outlander PHEV commands and its so-so performance, though it’s updated for 2027 with more power. It also has plenty of features, decent interior quality, and a healthy 45-mile electric range. Along with the regular Outlander, it’s also the only three-row SUV in the compact segment.

As the only series hybrid in the mainstream segment, Nissan has made a big splash with the Rogue Hybrid after more than a decade without any gas-electric powertrain in its lineup. Think of the company’s e-Power hybrid setup like an extended-range EV where the gas engine serves only as a generator for the electric motors, but without the plug or the big battery. We like how it drives—a lot.

Porsche’s conventional hybrid powertrain sits in its most prized product, the 911, where the T-Hybrid installs one or two electric turbos and a small battery on the GTS and Turbo S. The models with the E-Hybrid badge are plug-in hybrids. The Panamera has three PHEV choices, including the Turbo’s V-8 powertrain shared with Bentley for up to 771 horsepower. The Cayenne Hybrid has either a V-6 hybrid setup or a similar V-8 setup in either the SUV or Coupe body style.

#4209. NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test

NASA has successfully completed another powerful rocket engine test as the agency prepares for future Artemis missions that will return astronauts to the Moon and lay the groundwork for human exploration of Mars.

On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center, located near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The developmental engine ran for its full scheduled duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

Although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data. Engineers will use the results to improve the power, efficiency, and reliability of RS-25 engines designed for upcoming Artemis missions.

Powerful RS-25 Engines Will Help Send Astronauts Back to the Moon

NASA is preparing for Artemis IV, a mission scheduled for 2028 that aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface. The mission will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, using the massive Space Launch System (SLS) rocket to carry astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft.

Artemis IV represents an important step toward NASA's larger ambitions. The agency plans to explore the Moon's South Pole, establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, and develop the experience and technologies needed for the first crewed journey to Mars.

The RS-25 engines play a crucial role in making these missions possible. Each SLS rocket uses four of the engines, which together generate up to 2 million pounds of thrust to help propel the spacecraft off the launchpad and into space.

Before any RS-25 engine is cleared for flight, it must undergo testing at NASA's Stennis Space Center to verify that it can perform reliably under the extreme conditions of a rocket launch.

These tests are carried out by specialists from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions, working together to ensure the engines are ready to power future journeys beyond Earth.

#4208. Narrowed Focus: 1997 Toyota Camry LE Tested

One of America’s favorite family haulers gets a full makeover.

Over 3,000,000 sold! Call it the McCamry. Along with the Ford Taurus and the Honda Accord, this Toyota is right at the top of the list when Amer­ican families go new-car shopping, and right at the top of the ratings in our last family-sedan comparison test (November 1995). Since its introduction here in 1983, Toyota has diligently smoothed up, slicked up, and suaved up the Camry till the only remaining awkwardness is the unlikely spelling of its name.

That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite. We’re talking refinement of the Camry theme, not reinvention. In fact, the basic platform and powertrain carry on, though engineering improvements seem to touch every part of the car. It’s slightly bigger in each exterior dimension—0.7 inch longer, 0.4 inch wider, 2.1 inches longer in wheelbase; the same four­-cylinder and V-6 engines are modestly more powerful (up 8 hp in the four, up 6 hp in the V-6); and the interior has been upgraded to meet all the safety standards scheduled in the next few years, including the 1997 side-impact and 1999 head-­impact requirements. The aerodynamic drag coefficient has been improved to 0.30, from 0.33.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 75078

Toyota is, however, tightening the Camry’s focus. It’s available only as a four-door now in three trim levels: CE, LE, and XLE. Gone is the coupe, which won over just five percent of Camry buyers. Gone, too, is the station wagon, a shape that convinced only three per­cent of Camry buyers in its losing battle against the tide of minivans. (Production of a Camry-based minivan begins next spring.)

In the past, we’ve joked that the Camry’s personality is one of aggressive bland­ness. Unlike the frisky feeling of the Accord and the athletic tautness of the Dodge Intrepid, both of which come through loud and clear before you’ve driven to the first corner, the Camry’s subtlety grows on you over time. It’s smoother, softer, quieter than the others, less com­municative, less mechanical. Instead of talking to you in the very pleasant way of those others, it’s the silent type that, you soon notice, goes expertly about its job.

In this new Camry, Toyota sharpened the expertise without changing the per­sonality. It’s still a car that’s light to the touch: easy to steer, easy to brake. The ride is commendably free of harshness, thanks in part to mounting the suspension on isolated crossmembers front and rear. The four­-cylinder version, with its 195/70SR-14 tires, rides very smoothly and ignores almost completely the road textures that create so much droning in sporting cars. The V-6s come with 205/65HR-15s on six­-inch-wide wheels. These tires are noticeably harsher and noisier than those on the four-cylinder cars, though road nose is still quite reasonable when compared with other cars in this class. Road grip and handling predictability are well above the minimums we’d set for family cars.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 75078

The Camry V-6 has been one of the top performers in this class. The 1997 model gains six horsepower (now 194 hp at the same 5200 rpm as the previous peak), gets shorter final-drive gearing (3.93 versus 3.43), and weighs about the same as last year’s smaller car. Another performance plus: A manual transmission has returned to the V-6 lineup, available only on CE models. How­ever, our LE V-6 auto­matic was no quicker than the last LE V-6 we tested, managing 0 to 60 mph in 8.3 seconds. Expect the five-speed to trim that by about four-tenths.

On the road, the automatic’s eagerness to change down a gear or two when you press the pedal, even slightly, and the seamless smoothness of those changes give this car quick reflexes in traffic. The engine revs with the hushed moan of a Lexus. This year, traction control is optional on LE and XLE V-6 models. When it comes to powertrain pleasures, the Camry is world-class.

Still, it’s the more subtle details of pas­senger accommodation that make this Toyota a family favorite. In the previous­-generation Camry, our comparison tests show two adults fit in the back seat more comfortably than in some other brands up to 10 inches longer. We expect this Camry advantage to widen fractionally in this new model because both legroom and head­room in back are increased by a half-inch. Although the Camry is wider on the out­side, energy-absorbing padding to protect in side impacts takes up the extra space and, in certain spots, a little more. The Camry still has pockets in the front doors, unlike the Taurus, which sacrificed them for crash-protection equipment.

Those who wish to maximize rear-seat space should think twice about opting for power front seats (standard equipment on the top-of-the-line XLE). The manual­adjust buckets have excellent toeroom under them, which the power adjuster interrupts with a transverse bar. Tall folks won’t like that.

As in most modern sedans, the Camry has fold-forward rear seatbacks split one­-third and two-thirds, allowing the cargo compartment to be extended into the pas­senger area. Here’s another think-twice: Camrys equipped with the optional child seat—it’s built into the two-thirds section of the rear seat—have that section fixed in place, ruling out all but a narrow passage into the trunk.

At the rear, the trunklid opens wider and lower than before. Space inside, however, is a bit less in the new body—14.1 cubic feet versus 14.8 before. And the new car still has the conventional trunk hinges with the sickle arms that swing down into your luggage when the lid is closed.

Conventional is the right description for the new instrument panel, certainly more conventional than the old one, which tried to visually compartmentalize the cockpit by emphasizing a huge black field in front of the driver. That was the good part. The bad part was the deemphasized and totally boring padding it left for the passenger’s amusement. Now the all-new panel stretches its padding across the inte­rior in an equal-opportunity gesture that makes the interior seem brighter and wider. The glove box is 29 percent larger. The audio controls were raised to a mid­dash height, making them easy to see and reach. The climate controls have changed over to the increasingly common turn-to-adjust knobs. They’re large enough, and so obvious in their workings, that they are easy to operate in their less prominent location. The Camry continues to position its ignition switch in the dash where you can readily see it, instead of hiding it on the side of the steering column.

Toyota has proven itself to be the master of those little conveniences that add up to an exceptionally pleasing car. In this new Camry we see more clever trade-offs as the engineers cut costs, reduce weight, and usually end up serving the customer better, too. For example, the new front bumper cuts the part count nearly in half and saves weight, yet it increases protec­tion to 5 mph from 2.5. Inside, the seats recline in stepless increments now, and the buckets’ height adjusters use a single knob instead of two. Both of these changes cut costs, Toyota says. We say they make the car better, too. Models that previously would have had retracting antennas now have the antenna screened on the rear glass, saving weight and cost. The new Bosch anti-lock brake system weighs half as much as the old one.

Still, not every cost saver is a benefit. The LCD odometer is simply gray num­bers on a gray field, making it less visible than the glowing digits in competitors like the Chrysler Cirrus and the Dodge Stratus. And the new one-piece front-bumper cover now incorporates the grille into its overtly ordinary Rubbermaid-looking façade.

There’s been much speculation in the automotive-trade press about a possible price cut. Don’t hold your breath. Sales of the old Camry hit records earlier this year with no apparent price cutting. Were there sweeteners for the dealer? Sure, but other brands had them, too. Toyota knows all the tricks for selling cars without collapsing its price structure-tricks, we think, that mostly won’t be needed to move this shrewdly updated Camry.

#4207. Nioh 3 launches, immediately becomes the most played Nioh ever on Steam

Just a few hours after launch, Nioh 3 is already the biggest release in series history on Steam.

It sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

At the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

This already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

#4206. 2026 Nominations Open For Awards Show GTA 6 Can’t Sweep

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

Last week saw the grand unveiling of the nominees for this year’s Game Awards, and to nobody’s particular surprise, it was absolutely papered in Grand Theft Auto 6 from head to toe. Now, I’m not saying Grand Theft Auto 6 doesn’t deserve its flowers, it very much does, but considering it’s more or less a forgone conclusion that it’s gonna sweep the entire show, it kinda takes the fun out of it. 2026 has been a pretty good year for gaming, all things considered, and we need some awards that properly showcase that. In other words, a set of awards that GTA 6 cannot sweep.

Well, as it so happens, nominations have just opened today for the 2026 Steam Awards, a yearly showcase of the best and brightest in PC gaming, at least as far as games available on Valve’s popular platform go. You know what’s not on PC, let alone on Steam? Grand Theft Auto 6. That makes the Steam Awards a slightly better opportunity for the rest of the year’s standouts, especially those in the indie scene, to strut their stuff.

Nominations will be open until November 30, after which the actual voting process will begin on December 17. The winners will then be announced on January 2. If you’ve got any PC games you want to highlight, now’s the time to do it.

The 10 Rules for Surviving a Seasonal Steam Sale will ensure you get through with some new games and an intact wallet.

For those unfamiliar with how this process works, it’s pretty straightforward. For this initial step, you can nominate pretty much any game you want for all but two of the Steam Awards’ 14 categories. Whether you played it or not, it doesn’t matter. If it’s on Steam and was released after last year’s Autumn Sale, it’s eligible.

Said categories include “Best Handheld Game” for a game best played on a Steam Deck, “Just Five More Minutes” for hideously addictive games that keep you going and going, “Defies Description” for delightfully odd games that don’t quite fit any single genre, “This is My Job Now” for games that simulate jobs and professions, “Better with Friends” for multiplayer stuff, “Best Game You Suck At” for difficult games, “Six Back and Relax” for chill, cozy games, and the self-explanatory “Outstanding Story-Rich,” “Outstanding Visual Style,” and “Best Soundtrack” categories.

For this initial step, you can nominate pretty much any game you want for all but two of the Steam Awards’ 14 categories.

Besides all that, we also have the coveted title of Game of the Year, for which any game that really defined 2026 for you is elligible, as well as VR Game of the Year, which is the same but, y’know, for VR games.

One of the two categories with special rules is “Labor of Love,” which is only open to games that have been around since before the 2025 Steam Autumn Sale. That one’s specifically for titles that have been kept afloat through an abundance of new content and/or developer support.

The other special award category, and this is where things are going to get interesting this year, is a newcomer for the Steam Awards: the “Hall of Fame.” As the Steam Awards got their start back in 2016, there are now exactly 10 Game of the Year winners dating back to its conception. The Hall of Fame category is the only category with specified candidates for nomination, from which the finalists will be selected based on player input.

Those candidates are, starting from the first Game of the Year winner, Grand Theft Auto 5, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, PUBG Battlegrounds, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Red Dead Redemption 2, Resident Evil Village, Elden Ring, Baldur’s Gate 3, Black Myth Wukong, and Hollow Knight: Silksong. I hope everyone is wearing protective gear, because this is going to be contentious, to put it nicely.

Once again, remember to get your nominations in before November 30. If you nominate a game for every category (or skip categories you have no opinion on,) as well as play and review at least one nominated game, you’ll get a nifty Steam Badge, if you’re into that.

Steam gift cards will no longer be available at retail stores.

#4204. Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

"These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease."

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's

More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.

Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is important for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role

"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology."

The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

That distinction could be important for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments

"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential."

The findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an important opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration."

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal

The research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.

"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science."

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.

Materials provided by University of Virginia Health System. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4203. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

#4202. 2028 Honda CR-V Is a Fuel-Sipping Hybrid Family SUV Worth Waiting For

Honda’s bestseller goes hybrid only as it enters its seventh generation and will arrive in 2027 with a fresh design inside and out.

Honda’s bestselling model—and the third-bestselling vehicle in the United States through the third quarter of 2026—is getting a complete makeover. The CR-V will follow the path set forth by the sixth-generation Toyota RAV4, going hybrid only as the CR-V enters its seventh generation for the 2028 model year.

We expect the 2028 CR-V Hybrid to wear a sharp new design, with spy photos showing slim daytime running lights above a series of thin horizontal grilles, while the rear end features a light bar that stretches the full width of the SUV. It will likely also be the first vehicle in the U.S. to wear Honda’s new “H” logo, which was originally introduced for its future EVs but will now be applied to other vehicles in its lineup after Honda hurriedly canceled said EVs earlier this year.

The cabin is also expected to get a significant makeover, with the Avancier—a three-row SUV sold in Asia—providing hints about what to expect. The Avancier skips out on most real buttons and knobs, instead putting nearly every function into a large screen mounted to the dashboard, a dramatic shift from Honda’s current setup that prioritizes physical controls. The Avancier’s interior is wrapped in white upholstery, accented by glowing ambient lighting, and features a squared-off steering wheel. Honda also appears to be switching to a column-mounted gear selector.

See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 95361

While Honda was once led by the Accord and Civic sedans, in today’s SUV-obsessed market, the CR-V has become the Japanese automaker’s most important model. Its biggest rival, the RAV4, was overhauled for 2026 and went hybrid only. Now, the CR-V will follow suit to stay competitive in the incredibly crowded compact SUV segment. Hybrid sales of the current-generation CR-V have been strong, accounting for over half of the SUV’s total sales so far this year, making it a perfect choice to launch Honda’s new platform and hybrid powertrain.

The CR-V will arrive on a new platform that Honda promises will be stiffer and lighter than before, taking a modular approach that will lead to greater parts sharing and reducing costs. This platform will presumably be adapted to underpin future versions of the Accord and Civic, along with Acura models such as the upcoming next-generation RDX Hybrid.

Honda will ditch the standard 190-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine for the 2028 CR-V, which will arrive exclusively with the company’s new hybrid powertrain. The fifth generation of Honda’s two-motor hybrid setup will continue to use an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder, along with a pair of electric motors, but the 2.0-liter engine will be a fresh design, featuring a new cooling system. As before, the electric motors will power the wheels most of the time, but the gas engine can also be engaged to directly drive the wheels.

See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 95361

The electric motors are more compact than before, and Honda has developed a new battery too. The company says the new hybrid setup will bring improved power and efficiency, targeting 10 percent better fuel economy than the outgoing hybrid powertrain. The current CR-V Hybrid makes 205 horsepower and is rated at up to 38 mpg combined. We wouldn’t be surprised to see power increase to over 220 hp—the RAV4 makes 226 hp in FWD form and 236 hp with AWD—and fuel economy nudge up to just over 40 mpg.

The CR-V is expected to come with front-wheel drive standard and all-wheel drive optional, although it’s unclear if the latter will see the addition of a third electric motor. Honda will also likely include the S+ Shift feature seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, which simulates a traditional transmission’s gearchanges and allows the driver to manually shift with the steering-wheel paddles.

The CR-V’s chief rival will continue to be the Toyota RAV4. However, the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid and Nissan Rogue Hybrid, which both enter a new generation for 2027, will also be strong competitors. The Jeep Cherokee, Kia Sportage Hybrid, and Subaru Forester Hybrid will be in the mix too, along with nonhybrid compact SUVs like the Volkswagen Tiguan.

The move to only offer a hybrid powertrain could see the CR-V’s entry price climb, which might alienate some buyers. Honda will also need to make sure it can match or exceed the efficiency of rivals like the RAV4 while still providing adequate performance and a spacious, usable cabin, given how closely matched the compact SUV space is these days. Moving away from physical interior controls could also upset the Honda faithful who are used to the company’s simple-to-use buttons.

Production is set to kick off at Honda’s factories in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana, in April 2027. Sales should begin shortly after, and with the current CR-V Hybrid starting at $37,580, we expect the next-generation model to come in at around $38,000.

#4201. Ineos to Build Grenadiers in America and Sell Its French Plant to BYD

The fledgling automaker could start manufacturing its off-road-centric vehicles in the United States as soon as 2028.

The Ineos Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup truck could be trading the French-flag badges that signal their Hambach production for ones that feature America’s stars and stripes. That’s because the fledgling British automaker has now confirmed plans to begin building its vehicles in the United States, with the first American-made Ineos models scheduled for 2028.

Ineos Automotive is still determining the exact location of its planned American production facility, but it says that it has developed a shortlist of potential sites. The move will bring the brand’s production to its largest market, with the United States making up around 70 percent of Ineos’s global sales.

See all results for new 2027 Ineos Grenadier Quartermaster for sale near 75214

Since Ineos already sells most of its vehicles in the U.S., the move will help make the brand more efficient. By building its vehicles in America, Ineos will also be able to avoid paying many of the lofty import tariffs that it’s currently subjected to. Plus, along with announcing plans to move to the United States, Ineos confirmed it’s in the process of selling its current Hambach facility to Chinese automotive giant BYD.

At this point, Ineos hasn’t announced whether it plans to buy an existing manufacturing facility, build a new one, or use another automaker’s excess capacity. One thing Ineos has been clear about, though, is that the move will cover its entire global production. A final decision on the facility is expected within the next few months to keep the move on schedule.

#4198. AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.

Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.

The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.

AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records

Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.

Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.

To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.

The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.

AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases

The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.

The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.

For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.

These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.

Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.

Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.

Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).

This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.

For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.

PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."

"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."

Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?

The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.

Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.

"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.

"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."

Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.

"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.

Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.

"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.

"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."

The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.

The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.

The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

#4197. Grand Theft Auto 6 Easter Egg Traps Player In Squid Game

Scott Baird is a Contributor from the UK with over a decade of video game writing experience.

A disturbing Easter Egg has been discovered in Grand Theft Auto 6, one that traps the player in a life-or-death situation inspired by franchises like Saw and Squid Game, leading to a battle with a murderer.

The Grand Theft Auto series is well-known for its movie parodies and media references, some of which break the game’s realistic setting and move into sci-fi or supernatural territory. This has led players on wild-goose chases in search of UFOs, Bigfoot, and sea monsters, some of which do exist in the Grand Theft Auto universe.

One thing that definitely exists in the Grand Theft Auto universe is killers, with the protagonist being the worst of the bunch. Grand Theft Auto 6 has a far more calculated murderer than most, in a sequence discovered by The Easter Egg Hunter YouTube channel, one who can trap the player in a deadly game.

Some references are a little subtle in Grand Theft Auto 6, and some absolutely aren't. If you've ever wanted to get held up by Tom Cruise, now is your chance!

In Grand Theft Auto 6, it’s possible to encounter a woman with a broken arm in a cast, who is trying to move furniture into a van. If the player helps her, they get knocked out with a stun gun. This references a scene in the movie The Silence of the Lambs, where the killer Buffalo Bill captures his victims this way.

It’s possible to escape this scenario by walking away or killing the woman, but those who are trapped wake up in a storage container with a bomb on their neck. They are mocked through a speaker, similar to Jigsaw in Saw, and prompted to take part in a survival game.

The player is trapped on an island, with weapons and items strewn around, and a killer on the loose. This begins a battle royale-style scenario, where the player goes one-on-one with the killer, with the hunter becoming the hunted, much like in Squid Game.

It’s possible to escape this scenario by walking away or killing the woman, but those who are trapped wake up in a storage container with a bomb on their neck.

Unfortunately for the person planning the hunt, they didn’t count on facing a Grand Theft Auto protagonist, who can brutally turn the tables and kill their captor. Winning the game gets the player their items back, along with a cash prize and a boat that’ll let them return to the mainland.

The Grand Theft Auto series loves its references, and the hunted game packs multiple in at once. While fans are still waiting for news of Grand Theft Auto 6’s online component, this game feels like something that could appear as a battle mode, though people will quickly compare it to Fortnite and similar titles.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a gargantuan game, one that took a long time to develop. As of the time of writing, the game has been out for less than a week, but fans are already uncovering all kinds of secrets, including the ability to travel back to the PS2 era via a magic portal. This is just scratching the surface, especially as most fans haven’t even finished the main storyline yet.

It took years for fans to work out all the secrets in Grand Theft Auto 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2, and there’s a good chance that Grand Theft Auto6 will also be teasing fans with its hidden content for a long time. This will only get worse when the online component begins, and Rockstar can keep adding content for players to puzzle over for the next decade.

Even with the many easter eggs in GTA 6, you wouldn't expect time travel to be one of them. But you can do it if you're persistent enough to follow a meticulously planned order of steps.

#4195. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

The Mortality’s Tenderness banner features five new limited-time 5-Star Memories, one each for the game’s five love interests. The theme is all about warmth, reunion, and intimacy, taking place in a Wuxia-inspired setting that's once again an alternate universe from the main story of the game.

Furthermore, if you log in for 10 days throughout the event, you can unlock a new outfit set, Wealth Overflow, which can be worn by any of the love interests as well as the heroine. There are other login rewards, too, like 10 Deepspace Wishes, 10 Empyrean Wishes, His and My Outfit sets, two dynamic portrait photo poses, and loads more.

Finally, the Golden Fortune event adds even more daily log in rewards in the form of one free "shake" per day, from which you can earn a random reward of between 68 and 108 Diamonds — that adds up to a total of 1,296 Diamonds if you show up every day.

#4192. Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to new research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

The findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History

Published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

The scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how quickly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

Scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

To investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

For the new analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades

The results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Each new mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

Researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more quickly.

This consistency could have important medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

In at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep."

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer showed the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

This finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now."

He added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia."

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

Dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

"As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways."

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

She added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible."

Years of Blood Samples Unlock New Cancer Clues

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

"While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement."

The women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

The findings also showed that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

According to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

The next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.
