#4143. Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug. Even more concerning, the difference becomes substantially larger with age, reaching more than six years among people who develop psychosis in their 30s or later.

The findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney. They suggest that the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use may extend well beyond adolescence and could become more pronounced with prolonged exposure.

Psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations, false beliefs known as delusions, and disturbances in thinking or behavior. It can occur in schizophrenia and several other mental health disorders. Although psychosis most commonly begins during the late teenage years or early adulthood, it can develop at other stages of life. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults will experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

Cannabis Linked to Earlier Psychosis Across Adulthood

To investigate the relationship between cannabis use and the timing of psychosis, researchers at UNSW Medicine analyzed 149 studies involving more than 71,000 participants. Most of the research had been conducted since 2011 in Europe, North America, and Australia, with the majority of studies focusing on people diagnosed with schizophrenia.

The researchers discovered that the difference in the age at which psychosis first appeared varied considerably across age groups.

In studies where the average age of psychosis onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis users experienced their first episode approximately 1.6 years earlier than non-users. That difference widened to 4.43 years in studies involving people whose psychosis emerged in their mid-to-late 20s (25-29).

The largest difference appeared in studies where psychosis developed at age 30 or later. In this group, cannabis users experienced the condition an average of 6.3 years earlier than non-users.

These results suggest that the association between cannabis and earlier psychosis may become stronger as people grow older, potentially reflecting the effects of longer periods of cannabis exposure.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW's School of Clinical Medicine, said the findings raise important questions about the long-term psychiatric effects of cannabis.

"We've tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn't disappear once you're in your 20s," Prof. Large said. "What we're seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine."

Interestingly, the analysis did not identify a statistically significant difference in the timing of psychosis between teenage cannabis users and teenagers who did not use cannabis.

However, the researchers cautioned that this finding does not necessarily mean younger cannabis users face no risk. Psychosis rarely develops before the middle teenage years, leaving relatively little opportunity for its onset to shift to an even younger age.

"There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect," Prof. Large said.

The researchers also stressed an important limitation. Because the analysis examined existing observational studies, it cannot establish that cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes the condition begin sooner. Demonstrating such a relationship experimentally would require research that deliberately exposed people to potential psychiatric harm, which would be unethical.

Nevertheless, Prof. Large believes the overall pattern provides meaningful evidence supporting a possible causal connection.

"But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis."

New Findings Challenge Assumptions About Cannabis After Age 25

The latest research builds on two earlier investigations into cannabis use and the development of psychosis.

In a smaller 2011 meta-analysis led by Prof. Large, researchers found that psychosis began approximately 2.7 years earlier among cannabis users. A separate 2015 analysis reported that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began.

However, neither earlier investigation had enough information to determine how the relationship differed across age groups.

By incorporating a much larger body of research, the new analysis allowed scientists to examine how the association changes across different stages of adulthood.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW's School of Biomedical Sciences, said the findings undermine the idea that avoiding cannabis during adolescence is sufficient to eliminate its potential psychiatric dangers.

"What we've found challenges the assumption that you'll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that's just not the case," Ms. Stevens said.

"There's been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone."

Why Even a Few Years of Delayed Psychosis Matter

Although a difference of two or three years might initially seem relatively small, the researchers emphasized that the timing of psychosis can have profound consequences for a person's future.

The late teenage years and early adulthood are often periods when people complete their education, begin careers, establish relationships, and develop greater independence. Experiencing a serious psychiatric disorder earlier in life can interrupt these important milestones.

"People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel, and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well," Ms. Stevens said.

Prof. Large emphasized the potential benefits of reducing or discontinuing cannabis use and the importance of delaying the onset of psychosis wherever possible.

"It's a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you," he said. "If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline."

The potential benefits could also extend to healthcare systems. According to Prof. Large, psychotic disorders account for as much as 3% of health-related spending in developed countries. Preventing or delaying the onset of these conditions could therefore have substantial social and economic benefits.

Scientists Call for Stronger Cannabis Health Warnings

Despite the inability to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship, the researchers believe their findings provide sufficient justification for stronger warnings about the possible psychiatric consequences of cannabis use.

"We can't run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available," Prof. Large said. "In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met."

One concern is the growing popularity of medical cannabis. Prof. Large said its increasing use as a therapeutic product may encourage some people to assume that it carries little risk.

He has also observed an increasing number of patients receiving treatment for psychosis who had previously been prescribed cannabis for medical conditions where evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited.

"It's got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk."

Another emerging concern involves cannabis edibles, which can contain elevated concentrations of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for the drug's mind altering effects. The availability of products containing higher THC concentrations raises additional questions about possible psychiatric risks.

At the same time, Prof. Large acknowledged that cannabis legalization could create opportunities to reduce harm, even though it would also make cannabis easier to obtain.

Legal regulation could allow governments to establish limits on product potency, improve consumer education, introduce taxation, and require buyers to receive clear information about potential health consequences.

"You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying," Prof. Large said.

More Research Needed on Long-Term Cannabis Exposure

The researchers say further studies are necessary to understand the biological processes that might explain why the association between cannabis use and earlier psychosis becomes more pronounced with age.

In particular, they want to investigate whether repeated or prolonged cannabis exposure produces cumulative changes that influence when psychotic symptoms emerge.

They also recommend additional research focusing on older cannabis users, an increasingly important population as medical cannabis becomes more common and products containing high concentrations of THC become more widely available.

Another priority is improving how cannabis exposure is measured. The researchers argue that future studies need clearer and more consistent methods for recording cannabis consumption so that findings can be compared more reliably.

Ultimately, the new analysis highlights an important gap in public understanding of cannabis and mental health. While warnings have traditionally concentrated on teenage use, the findings suggest that potential psychiatric risks deserve attention throughout adulthood, particularly among people who continue using cannabis over many years.

Materials provided by University of New South Wales. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4142. Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business Review - Delivering Where It Matters

Australia Did It: End-of-the-world Railway Defense Business is a game I catch myself playing in my head long after I shut it off. Though it uses turn-based strategy as its base, it expands beyond the genre’s regular confines, blending elements from roguelikes, puzzle games, bullet-heaven titles, and the tower-defense genre. The result is an experience that demands wide-scale experimentation and rewards improvisation.

In a post-apocalyptic world where the Atlantic Ocean has dried up, you risk your life to ensure your shipment reaches its destination. Riding from station to station by train, you must build your team amid your many missions as various mutated creatures, malicious machines, and coordinated soldiers attack your convoy. Lore is doled out piecemeal and serves mostly as background dressing, but each time I learned more about the world, I became more curious.

To survive the harshness of the wasteland, you must use cindermint, an in-game resource gained for surviving turns and killing enemies, to spawn defenders, with three base classes to choose from. The revolver-wielding Gunslinger is your primary damage dealer, while the Radshot applies corrosive radiation damage, and the Nomad offers a close-range shotgun blast with knockback.

Those base-level characters offer solid variety upon which to build. And that’s where the main hook for Australia Did It comes in: experimentation through combination. In the midst of battle, you can merge two units of the same level to create new, more powerful defenders, influenced by the traits of those used in the merge. At the onset, you can merge two Nomads to create a level 2 Nomad with increased damage and knockback, but the real fun comes in combining disparate units to create completely new characters. Even now, more than 15 hours into my gameplay, I’m still concocting new combinations I want to try on my next run.

By the end of my first successful run, I had multiple level 6 characters, including a railgun-toting heavy, mages who steal health from enemies and redistribute it to nearby allies, a drone that can move beyond the walls of the station to attack enemies directly, and, my personal favorite, a dual-shotgun-wielding one-man wrecking crew. However, many of these higher-level units also possess drawbacks to consider, like the railgun scorching all adjacent tiles or the drone running out of battery if it’s outside the walls for too long. Though I started keeping notes in my head about which combinations led to my favorite results, I was grateful for a comprehensive compendium that tracked the tens of unit types I unlocked through this rewarding experimentation.

The meat of the experience places your squad on a 25-tile square board with enemies spawning from the four principal directions. Thoughtfulness and positioning are crucial, as each unit on your squad possesses different traits and movement efficiency, as do the encroaching enemies. Basic enemies often make a beeline toward the station, while others may take a weaving route or keep their distance and blast you at range. Improvising and adjusting your strategy on the fly is the most engaging part of Australia Did It, and when you perfectly adapt in the moment, or escape the scenario by the skin of your teeth, there are few better feelings I’ve experienced in a game this year.

Your goal in this phase is to simply defend the station and gather resources to strengthen your squad before evacuating and moving on to the next area. Considering each unit's strengths, weaknesses, and capabilities while strategically positioning them around the station takes some getting used to, especially during the more chaotic stages. I fist-pumped as I watched the train pull out of a station that was about to crumble, and I lamented the loss of high-level units I had to leave behind to ensure the survival of the convoy. The process is ceaselessly thrilling, even as you begin to see how the gears work under the hood. I just wish I could say the same about the intervening train sections.

Once you escape the turn-based strategy portion, your surviving squad members hop aboard the train and chart their route. Using a basic map, you choose your next stop, with factors like enemy types and modifiers shown to you ahead of time. The top-down train segments between station-defense stages are largely passive; the units you evacuated from the previous station automatically attack swarming enemies with the same traits and perks they have in the main gameplay areas. You can aim a focus cone to instruct your units, but you’re at the mercy of the units you’ve brought. You can trigger an ultimate ability to send your defenders into overdrive, but I rarely needed it.

While I love the idea of intentionally crafting a team that’s good at both the turn-based strategy and bullet-heaven transport sections, I was never fully engaged getting from point A to point B. Instead, I often caught myself checking how much longer before my train arrived at the next station; these sections can be completed in a minute or two, but that doesn’t alleviate the feeling that it’s a step down from the other gameplay. These novel portions aren’t bad by any means; they’re merely an average part of an otherwise excellent experience.

Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world.

#4141. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4140. 10 Best Early Game Weapons in GTA VI

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

In Vice City, you can never come too prepared for a fight. Between the nightlife and our protagonist's penchant for causing chaos, it’s a good idea to stay strapped in case of an emergency.

The only issue is that in those opening hours, you’re pretty limited in what you can get because money is fairly tight. If you’re looking to buy guns, you don’t want to waste your money on something that feels suboptimal.

ATM machines hold a lot of cash in GTA 6. Learn how to break them open and steal everything inside with this guide.

This list includes a bunch of good weapons you can get in the first couple of chapters of the game. It feels a little crazy that the early game can stretch so far in hours, but GTA 6 really is a humongous game.

The Duval Signature ES9 is basically a more powerful version of Jason’s starting weapon, and it’s a great weapon to keep on you at all times. While it is a sidearm, it can still be helpful in all kinds of situations.

The key part of this one is that it has incredibly high handling, meaning you’ll pretty much always hit what you aim for. In the early hours of the game, that can be the difference between life and death.

At a certain point in the game, you’ll be able to grab Donnie’s sidearm and keep it for yourself. This small but mighty weapon is great for people looking to take people out quickly at a shorter range.

You won’t be able to take on a whole army with it, but it fits nicely into an extra slot for when things start to get a little dicey. Donnie is a crazy guy, so it makes sense his gun is just a little crazy too.

Most people will probably feel like a sniper is relatively useless, especially when the cops start to roll up on you. For the most part, that’s true, but with this weapon you can easily take out some people without getting spotted.

With high range, accuracy, and decent damage, you can put down just about anything you come across with relative ease. Just be sure you’re far enough away to not have to worry about when people start looking.

This weapon is an alternative assault rifle you can buy called a battle rifle, and it comes in handy when going up against big crowds of enemies. Not only does it pack a good punch, but you can stay in relative safety while using it.

The only real downside to this one is that using it a little too much might see you moving in a negative way with your Criminal Profile. That’s probably something you’re going to want to avoid if you’re hoping to stick to a happy ending.

This lovely little piece does a great job at putting just about anything down, but you’ll still need to be choosy about how you fire. It does have great handling, but you could still find yourself in real danger if you get surrounded quickly.

Aside from that, it’s a great weapon for car fights since it can pack such a good punch. If you’ve got the aim to use it, this bad boy can take on most any challenge, except maybe some truly unhinged NPCs.

If you are having trouble finding yourself a plane in GTA VI, this guide is for you.

A fancy found weapon, the Scrapper VF5C, is a great weapon to get, especially before you start getting into the really crazy parts of the game. Silenced and ready for action, this gun will be a great tool for taking on even the toughest jobs.

It does lack some stopping power, but with such high handling, it’s relatively easy to use, and that’s a very good thing. As long as you’re smart with it, there’s virtually nothing this weapon can’t handle.

One of the best early-game weapons that you can grab basically right at the start is the Wortham W-14. It’s a little tough to use, but once you have the hang of it, you can put down anyone who crosses your path.

It’s a fantastic weapon, especially if you’re looking to keep your Criminal Profile on the lighter side. One shot is really all you need with this one, and with such high accuracy, it hardly ever misses the mark.

Probably the best early-game longarm weapon you can get, this found weapon will make swiss cheese out of anyone you want. It’s got high damage and good handling, but you’ll be on your own for aiming and distance.

This gun is phenomenal for almost any scenario, but especially in situations where you’re running into a lot of people. Whether it’s the foot or the face, you’ll only ever need to shoot once at someone to take them out of the fight.

Of course, it wouldn’t be a Rockstar game without including some choice references, and what a reference it is. With this lovely piece as a nod to Red Dead Redemption, you’ll find yourself operating like a real cowboy on the streets of Vice City.

The gun is only available as part of the Ultimate Edition, which is a little problematic, but despite that, it isn’t the only powerful early-game sidearm. It does pack quite the punch and lets you pick off enemies from a distance.

The best early-game weapon of all is a found weapon you can get from pretty much the opening hours of the game. This small silenced pistol is great for committing all kinds of nefarious acts without ever having to worry about getting caught.

While its damage is low, it’ll never give away your position and can quickly put holes in people with ease. It works best if you’re looking to avoid complete shootouts, but really you could pretty much use it whenever in this insanely good simulation game.

#4139. Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants. Researchers at the University of Sydney have discovered a subtype called "circadian depression," which appears to be closely connected to the body's internal biological clock.

The discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression. Nearly one-quarter of the participants in the study, which focused on people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, showed characteristics of this newly identified subtype.

Circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy. People with this form of depression tend to respond less favorably to common serotonin-based antidepressants. However, treatments that target the brain circuits involved in controlling circadian rhythms, including melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy, may offer more effective options.

Published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, the findings shed light on the genetic factors associated with this subtype and offer a possible explanation for why widely used medications such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are less effective for some patients.

A Hidden Type of Depression Affecting Nearly One in Four Patients Studied

To investigate the biological differences between forms of depression, researchers examined information collected through the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Their analysis included clinical histories and genetic data from more than 10,000 people who had experienced depression.

The researchers identified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Several recognizable patterns distinguished these individuals from other people with depression.

Those with the circadian subtype were more likely to experience seasonal changes in their depression, sleep for longer periods when depressed, and wake up feeling exhausted despite spending more time in bed. They were also more likely to be night owls, meaning they naturally preferred staying awake late and waking later in the day.

The differences extended beyond sleep patterns. Depression often began earlier in life for these individuals, and their symptoms tended to be more severe (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). Genetic analysis also revealed an increased predisposition to inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems, along with major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

First author Dr. Emiliana Tonini from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Center said:

"Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them."

Why Common Antidepressants May Be Less Effective

One of the most important implications of the discovery involves how depression is treated.

Medications such as SSRIs and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are generally among the first treatments offered to people diagnosed with depression. These drugs work by influencing chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate mood.

However, the researchers found that these medications tend to be less effective for people with circadian depression. Individuals with this subtype also experience more side effects, suggesting that conventional antidepressants may not be the best initial approach for everyone.

Because circadian depression is closely associated with the body's internal clock, therapies designed to influence that clock may be particularly useful. Light therapy, for example, uses controlled exposure to bright light to help regulate biological rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone involved in signaling when the body should prepare for sleep, and antidepressants that target melatonin pathways may also be relevant treatment options.

Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse from the Brain and Mind Center explained:

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances."

A New Approach Could Improve Depression Treatment in Young People

Recognizing circadian depression earlier could be especially important for younger patients, who may otherwise spend valuable time trying medications that are less suited to their particular form of depression.

Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist, warned that failing to identify this subtype in young people can contribute to unsuccessful early treatments and unnecessary side effects.

The findings highlight the importance of recognizing that depression is not a single, uniform condition. Different biological mechanisms may contribute to similar symptoms, meaning that treatments effective for one person may provide much less benefit to another.

By identifying patients whose depression is closely tied to circadian rhythms, clinicians may be able to offer more targeted treatments earlier rather than relying on the same initial medication approach for everyone.

"We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

"Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition."

#4138. New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

Researchers in Japan have developed a promising new treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. Unlike conventional approaches that can eliminate both good and bad bacteria, the new therapy is designed to target specific microbes responsible for damaging gums and the bone that supports teeth.

Developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light. Early experiments in human cell cultures and mice suggest that it could offer a more precise way to combat periodontitis, a serious form of gum disease that can eventually lead to tooth loss. The findings were published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems

The human mouth contains a complex community of microorganisms, many of which play important roles in maintaining oral health. Problems can arise when harmful bacteria multiply and disturb this delicate balance.

One particularly troublesome species is Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), which scientists classify as a keystone pathogen. This means it can have an outsized influence on the surrounding microbial community, even when it is not especially abundant. By promoting inflammation and disrupting the normal balance of oral bacteria, it can contribute to the destruction of the bone that holds teeth in place.

Treating periodontitis often involves eliminating the bacteria responsible for the infection. However, some existing antimicrobial treatments do not distinguish between harmful organisms and microbes that help maintain a healthy mouth.

"Current treatments for periodontitis, including antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT), eliminate both pathogenic and beneficial oral bacteria," said Kazuhide Sato, one of the corresponding authors and a lecturer at Nagoya University. "These approaches often disrupt the entire oral microbial ecosystem and can also release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that may exacerbate inflammation."

Scientists Adapt Cancer Therapy to Target Gum Disease Bacteria

To overcome these limitations, the Nagoya University team turned to a technology originally designed to treat cancer. Known as near-infrared photoimmunotherapy, it uses antibodies linked to a light-sensitive dye to recognize specific targets. Once the compound attaches to its intended target, exposure to near-infrared light activates the dye and produces a damaging effect.

The researchers adapted this strategy to attack P. gingivalis without unnecessarily disturbing other oral bacteria. Their approach relies on IgY, a type of antibody collected from the egg yolks of hens that have been immunized against the pathogen.

Egg yolk antibodies offer a practical advantage because they can be produced in large quantities at relatively low cost. This could make them an attractive option for developing targeted treatments that are affordable and scalable.

The resulting technology, called near-infrared photo-antibacterial targeting therapy (NIR-PAT²), was developed by researchers at Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine. The team included first author Hiroshi Maruyama, Professor Hideharu Hibi, and corresponding authors Sato and Kiyoshi Sakai.

To determine whether the treatment could destroy harmful bacteria while protecting healthy tissue, the researchers tested it in human cell cultures and mice. They also compared its effects with those of conventional antimicrobial therapies.

Light-Activated Antibodies Destroy Harmful Bacteria

Laboratory experiments showed that the antibody and dye combination attached specifically to P. gingivalis. Other bacterial species and healthy human gum cells were left unaffected.

When the researchers illuminated the targeted bacteria with near-infrared light, the activated dye damaged their outer membranes, ultimately killing them.

Microscopic examination revealed an important difference between this technique and conventional antimicrobial light therapy. Bacteria exposed to the new treatment developed tiny openings in their membranes but largely maintained their overall shape. By contrast, conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy caused the bacteria to break apart completely.

The distinction matters because destroying bacterial cells can release substances that contribute to inflammation. Preserving the overall structure of the targeted bacteria, even after killing them, could help limit this unwanted effect.

The researchers also examined how the treatments affected healthy human gum cells. Their targeted therapy caused no detectable harm to these cells, while conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy produced cellular damage and slowed healing.

The team next investigated whether these laboratory findings would translate into meaningful improvements in gum disease.

In mice with periodontitis, the experimental therapy significantly reduced the loss of alveolar bone, the part of the jawbone that surrounds and supports teeth. Preventing this type of bone deterioration is especially important because advanced periodontitis can loosen teeth and eventually cause them to fall out.

Analysis of the animals' saliva revealed another encouraging result. The treatment reduced P. gingivalis while preserving beneficial Streptococcus bacteria, helping maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms in the mouth.

Conventional antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, on the other hand, eliminated both harmful and beneficial bacteria in the experiments, causing broader disruption to the oral microbial community.

"Results demonstrated that, unlike antibiotics or standard light therapy, this approach selectively removes the primary pathogenic species while preserving the remainder of the oral bacterial community," Sato said.

Together, the findings suggest that targeting individual disease-causing bacteria could help control gum disease while avoiding some of the unintended consequences of broader antimicrobial treatments.

AI Could Help Develop More Precise Gum Disease Treatments

Although the early results are promising, the researchers recognize that periodontitis is a complex disease involving multiple bacterial species. Eliminating P. gingivalis alone may not be sufficient to treat every case.

To address this challenge, the team plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to examine publicly available information about oral bacteria. By identifying other important microorganisms and studying how different species interact, they hope to uncover additional targets for future therapies.

The researchers also see potential implications beyond oral health. Periodontitis has been linked to several other medical conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes.

Understanding the relationships between oral bacteria and these conditions could eventually help scientists identify which patients are most likely to benefit from specific treatments. AI analysis may play a role in making those decisions and guiding the development of more personalized approaches to gum disease.

For now, the therapy remains experimental, with its effectiveness demonstrated in laboratory studies and mice rather than human clinical trials. However, the findings point toward a possible future in which treating gum disease means selectively removing harmful bacteria instead of disrupting the entire microbial community that helps keep the mouth healthy.

Materials provided by Nagoya University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

PlayStation has reportedly canceled Fairgames, the long-in-development live-service shooter being made by Haven Studios, which Jade Raymond founded in 2021. Sony acquired Haven in 2022, and in 2025, Raymond left the studio, though it remained dedicated to developing Fairgames without her. It seems the story of Fairgames is now over, according to a new Bloomberg report.

The publication reports that PlayStation will not enforce any job cuts or layoffs as a result of Fairgames' cancellation, which comes as a surprise, and the studio will instead shift to support other first-party teams under the PlayStation umbrella. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle wrote in an email to employees today, according to Bloomberg. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Reading between the lines, many fans were waiting for news like today's cancellation of Fairgames to drop.

Still, in an era where games are canceled and entire teams are laid off (sometimes even after releasing a successful game), it's nice to see Haven employees are not facing layoffs.

#4133. IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes

An IBM quantum computer has completed an extraordinarily complex computational task in just 15 minutes, while leading methods for simulating the calculation on conventional computers would require prohibitively long runtimes. Perhaps even more significantly, researchers were able to establish statistical confidence in the accuracy of the quantum computer's results, addressing one of the biggest obstacles in the field.

The achievement, led by IBM and researchers from the University of Chicago, satisfies the fundamental criteria for quantum advantage. This milestone occurs when a quantum computer performs a computational task beyond the practical capabilities of leading classical computing methods while producing results that can be trusted.

In their new paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers demonstrated that both objectives could be achieved simultaneously using a novel design for encoded quantum circuits. The experiment represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing to date. The researchers have also made their circuits and experimental results publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.

Solving Quantum Computing's Verification Problem

Unlike conventional computers, which process information using bits that represent either zero or one, quantum computers rely on quantum bits, or qubits. These can exist in combinations of both states and interact through a phenomenon known as quantum entanglement. These properties allow quantum computers to approach certain computational problems in fundamentally different ways.

For years, scientists have tested the capabilities of quantum computers using a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS). This technique involves running a series of randomly selected quantum operations and generating samples from a complex probability distribution. As the circuits grow larger and more complicated, reproducing their output with a classical computer becomes increasingly difficult.

However, this approach creates a fundamental dilemma. If a computation is too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, how can researchers establish that the quantum computer performed it correctly?

As computational complexity increases, independently verifying the results becomes progressively more difficult and eventually impractical without making strong assumptions about how accurately the quantum hardware operates.

To overcome this problem, the IBM and University of Chicago team developed a more structured alternative to random circuit sampling. The researchers mathematically demonstrated that their approach preserves the same computational hardness criteria as conventional RCS while introducing a structure that allows errors to be detected during the computation.

"Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," said Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem."

Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers."

70 Logical Qubits and Tenfold Lower Error Rates

One of the greatest challenges in building powerful quantum computers is their extraordinary sensitivity to errors. Quantum information can be disrupted by environmental disturbances, imperfections in hardware, and inaccuracies in the operations used to manipulate qubits. As computations become longer and more complex, these errors can accumulate and undermine the reliability of the results.

Quantum error correction addresses this weakness by encoding quantum information across multiple physical qubits to create more reliable units known as logical qubits. This approach allows certain errors to be identified and, depending on the technique, corrected or accounted for without destroying the underlying quantum information.

In one of the largest known demonstrations of quantum error correction, the researchers performed computations using 70 protected logical qubits. The experiment involved 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates."

Quantum gates are the fundamental operations that manipulate quantum information, much like logic gates in conventional computers. Two-qubit gates allow qubits to interact, while T gates enable additional types of quantum operations needed for universal quantum computing. Together, these gate counts illustrate the considerable complexity of the experiment.

By encoding the quantum circuits, the researchers achieved effective logical error rates 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates. This substantial reduction allowed the quantum computer to maintain remarkably high fidelity, a measure of how closely the actual quantum state matches the intended one, despite performing thousands of complex operations.

"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a new foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically."

The researchers found that many leading classical simulation techniques would require impractically long periods to reproduce the computation. IBM's quantum computer, by comparison, accomplished the task in approximately 15 minutes.

Although the experiment was designed to demonstrate quantum advantage rather than solve an immediate real-world problem, it addresses two essential requirements for making large-scale quantum computing practical: controlling errors and establishing confidence in computational results.

By demonstrating both capabilities in a computation beyond the practical reach of leading classical methods, the researchers have taken a significant step toward a future in which quantum computers could reliably tackle scientific and industrial problems that are currently out of reach.

Materials provided by IBM. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4131. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

Discovery and Paramount Skydance (Skydance New Media is a game development branch of the now-merged Skydance Corporation).

Skydance Games told the development team behind Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra on Slack this afternoon that the game is not canceled, despite a widely circulated rumor on Twitter today claiming that it was.

Furthermore, Kotaku’s Rebekah Valentine clarified in her report that Marvel 1943 executive producer Lu Giglotti told staff in a Skydance Slack message he’d spoken directly with the executive leadership team to confirm Marvel 1943 is still alive, saying, "There is no truth to these claims." According to Kotaku’s report, Giglotti informed the team that Marvel 1943 was approaching an Alpha milestone later this month. Giglotti also told staff not to let the rumor distract them and that Skydance was "monitoring the situation" to address in the future.

Kotaku’s report also sheds light on the game’s tumultuous development cycle. Marvel 1943 was originally pitched as a Netflix game before it was eventually turned into a console and PC title. This transition means the current iteration is “light on gameplay” and lacks substantial interactions, with players primarily using a single button to play it.

This isn't a completely surprising revelation, as Marvel 1943 was billed as a narrative-driven, linear single-player experience when it was revealed, but the style of game has never been clear. The same reveal also saw Skydance promise the game boasted "intuitive controls and exhilarating second-to-second gameplay that captures the action and excitement of Marvel, inspired by landmark comics, television, and films, as they navigate this all-new globe-trotting adventure." This disconnect may be attributed to Kotaku also reporting that Marvel 1943 is “well over budget,” and its overall scope has been heavily scaled back. Regardless, the outlet’s source claims the game is “close to done.”

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was initially slated to launch in 2025. It was then delayed to early 2026 "to add more polish", according to Skydance, before being pushed again to an undetermined launch window. The game has no announced platforms.

Although Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra appears safe for now, other recent projects have not been as fortunate. Be sure to read our stories about the recent high-profile cancellations of Gang of Dragon and Fairgames.

#4128. You Can Play Japan’s Viral New Cat Petting Simulator Free in Your Browser Right Now

Greg has more than than 10 years of experience in video game journalism, covering some of the biggest games on the 8th and 9th generations of console.

If you’ve ever been at work or away from home and missing your furry feline friend, Japan’s latest obsession might just have you covered. Thanks to the power of technology, you can now happily pet cats through your internet browser and reduce your stress in a heartbeat.

As seen on Famitsu, Cat Petting Simulator (or Neko Nade Simulator as it’s known in Japan) has gone viral on social media, racking up over 53,000 reposts and 200,000 likes on X. Netizens from all over the world have been complimenting the game, made by a lone Japanese developer.

Cats in the Shell is bringing its bizarre combination of adorable pilots and war machines to PC, with Steam Early Access scheduled to begin in 2027.

Playing is as simple as opening the website, moving your mouse to maneuver the hand over the cat’s head and back, and voila! Watch the cat react with happy animations and purring feedback… if only we could get a haptic mouse that felt like fur. For added immersion, add something fluffy between your hand and mouse.

Customization is surprisingly deep for a browser game, allowing players to choose between more than 10 different coat colours and patterns (including solid black, white, calico and tabby). Chonky cat enthusiasts will be happy to hear that their needs will be met: players can adjust the cat’s size and thickness with handy sliders.

Players appear to have a soft spot for cat-driven adventures, be they more expansive like Stray, or even a simple casual game like Neko Atsume, which has attracted millions of smartphone gamers with its idle cat collecting gameplay.

Stray also had its viral moment when it first launched, with clips of the game spreading like wildfire on social media. Players fell in love with the game’s furry protagonist, its dedicated meow button and gritty environments populated with robot inhabitants. Consensus on the game was positive when it launched, but some have questioned whether people even played it before raving about it online.

In a month of gaming dominated by towering goliath titles like Grand Theft Auto 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, Cat Petting Simulator reminds us that cats remain one of gaming’s most reliable crowd-pleasers—and there’s no need for cutting edge graphics or physics.

These cat-themed games are sure to deliver the purrfect heartwarming, cozy game experience you are looking for.

#4127. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

#4124. Ahead of the Game - Sol Cesto is a creepy dungeon-diving roguelike with visuals you won't soon forget

It's all about descending into the darkness and discovering what lies in its depths in this week's Ahead of the Game series, where we tell you about a new mobile endeavour that's playable in one form or another despite its unofficial launch.

The idea of descending into the depths of the unknown is already terrifying as it is, but in Sol Cesto, you're doing so because the sun has mysteriously disappeared - and all manner of unholy creatures have taken over because of it.

I've always been a fan of roguelikes, so the genre alone already scores points in my book. But I suppose what makes Sol Cesto even more interesting are the visuals - in some ways, it reminds me of this Burton-esque puzzler, Jars, with its creepy-but-cute charm.

Now, there's absolutely nothing cute about the monsters in the dungeons here, but it's still pretty compelling to dive into the depths to take them on. The randomised elements come in grids and stages, where you can use rewards you earn to, as you might expect, strengthen your hero when you head back up to the surface after inevitably perishing.

You unlock more heroes as you go along too, with each one offering their own sets of skills depending on your play style.

The haunting music adds to the atmosphere, so if you're looking for horror-adjacent roguelike runs before rushing into December, this might just do the trick. So, how do you play Sol Cesto? It's currently got that "early access" tag on Google Play, but I'm curious as to what else Snapbreak is cooking up behind the scenes before this is officially launched. It's all pretty hush-hush at the moment, though, so if you want to get your hands on Sol Cesto before it's actually announced, now's your chance!

#4122. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#4121. 10 Video Game Rivals I Was Never Actually Mad At

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

Truth be told, I have a bit of a thing for villains who aren't entirely wrong. Give me an antagonist with a tragic backstory and a motive I can halfway get behind, and I will spend the entire final boss fight feeling a little bit bad about winning it. Some of the games on this list are old, which shows you how profoundly they impacted me at the time I played them.

From ideological masterminds to bombastic personalities, these 10 JRPG villains offer compelling stories and motives that can outshine the heroes.

I will say that most of these are still very much ultimately in the wrong. It’s usually their methods I have issues with, ranging from questionable to horrific. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Nonetheless, I can’t bring myself to be angry at them, because they are somewhat justified in their actions, so let's take a look at ten video game rivals I was never actually mad at.

Note: There are spoilers for every game on this list, including some very big ones.

N's whole philosophy is quite uncomfortable when you really think about it: he wants every Pokémon set free, because he believes they are suffering in the care of their trainers. And I'm not being funny, but he kind of has a point. We have spent 30 years catching animals, keeping them in tiny balls and making them fight each other for badges. The entire anime’s premise is that Pikachu didn’t like being stuck in a Poké Ball!

N is so very intriguing, right from the first encounter. Black and White had already given you two rivals in Cheren and Bianca before you even leave your hometown, and yet here is a third one, with his own battle theme and a design that looks nothing like anyone else's in a Pokémon game. He can also hear what Pokémon are saying, and when he tells you that yours genuinely like you, you believe him.

He reveals himself as the king of Team Plasma on the Ferris wheel in Nimbasa City, and later on, a legendary dragon chooses him without him ever throwing a single Poké Ball. You still beat him, though.

It then turns out that Ghetsis found him abandoned in the woods as a child, raised him alongside Pokémon that had been hurt by humans and turned him into a puppet king, all so Ghetsis could be the only person in Unova with Pokémon. The poor boy never stood a chance. As someone who will never play a Pokémon game without her starter, I'd like to think I'm one of the good ones, but I do understand his concerns.

Kirby: Nightmare in Dream Land is the rare case where the hero causes all the trouble. King Dedede steals the Star Rod from the Fountain of Dreams, breaks it into seven pieces and hands them out to his friends, and suddenly, nobody in Dream Land can dream anymore. Considering this is the same king who once stole all of Dream Land's food, Kirby assumes the worst, and quite frankly, I can't blame him.

The problem is that Kirby doesn't even let him explain. When the two of them meet at the fountain, Kirby refuses to listen to a single word and marches off to collect every piece. As far as we know, Dedede simply stays at the fountain the entire time, keeping an eye on things.

Then Kirby comes back, beats him and puts the Star Rod back in place, whilst Dedede hangs on to his feet and begs him not to. Out comes Nightmare, who Dedede had been keeping sealed away the whole time. Instead of saying "I told you so", he inhales Kirby and spits him into the sky to go and fix it, which is a lot more grace than I would have managed.

Lilith's backstory is a lot more relatable than you'd expect from the daughter of Mephisto. She was created as little more than an extension of her father, grew tired of the Eternal Conflict between Heaven and Hell, and ran off with the angel Inarius to create Sanctuary: a hidden world where renegade angels and demons could live in peace. They had a son, the others had children too, and those children became the Nephalem.

Now, the Nephalem turned out to be far more powerful than their parents, and that made the renegades nervous. Some of them argued that the children would draw the attention of Heaven and Hell and should be destroyed, and Lilith did not take that well: she hunted the renegades down and slaughtered angels and demons alike. A number of Nephalem died along the way, too, and I can’t lie: she kind of loses me here a little.

Subsequently, Inarius couldn't bring himself to kill her, so he banished her to the Void and used the Worldstone to weaken the Nephalem, which meant they eventually developed into what became mankind. I will note that her plans for her children weren't exactly selfless, either, since she always saw them as her own army. Still, the man she created them with was ready to wipe them out, and I can see how that might put someone in a bad mood for a few thousand years.

JRPGs sometimes put you on the other side of the good guy. Here are 8 PS2 JRPGs where you're actually the villain.

Maruki is the kind of man I'd trust with my problems instantly, which is exactly what makes him so difficult to fight. He joins Shujin Academy as the new school counsellor after the Kamoshida scandal, he is incredibly easy to talk to, and he genuinely wants to help. He's also a researcher in cognitive psience, which is never a good sign in Persona 5.

His story starts long before he meets the Phantom Thieves. When his girlfriend Rumi fell into a catatonic state after her parents were killed in a break-in, Maruki awakened a Persona that could rewrite cognition and used it to save her. It worked, but she forgot the trauma and him along with it, and he stepped out of her life so he wouldn't bring any of it back.

From there, his dream grew into a world without grief or suffering, where everyone gets the life they always wanted. The catch is that nobody gets asked: he convinced Sumire that she was her late sister Kasumi, and he'd happily do the same to everyone else. That takes away free will and the chance to grow through hardship, and he crossed that line long before we ever got involved. He isn't after money or power, though, and he truly believes he's helping, which is why his Palace was the one I least wanted to break into.

Sure, Sin is evil and the big bad, and thus the villain, but technically, we’re talking about every summoner who ever set out to destroy it. For hundreds of years, summoners travelled across Spira with a guardian or two, learned to call the aeons at every temple along the way and eventually made their way to Zanarkand for the Final Summoning. Once there, they would sacrifice a guardian to finally defeat Sin.

The problem is what happens afterwards. That guardian becomes the Final Aeon, and once Sin is destroyed, Yu Yevon possesses it and turns it into the next Sin. The Calm that everyone celebrates is really just the new Sin being created and slowly gaining its power, and so the whole cycle starts over again.

So why did they keep doing this for hundreds of years? Well, nobody knew until it was far too late. The sacrifice of the summoner and a guardian was common knowledge, but the fact that the guardian would become one with Sin was not, and summoners only learned the truth once they met Yunalesca in Zanarkand. By that point, you've gathered your aeons, travelled across the entire world and are about to go toe-to-toe with the biggest bad there is. I can't really blame a single one of them for going through with it.

Fou-Lu does not make a great first impression. Within minutes of waking up, he has two soldiers killed for bragging that the Fou Empire could crush dragons, and he looks rather pleased with himself about it. To be fair to him, he has just woken up from a centuries-long nap, and nobody is at their best first thing in the morning.

He is the God Emperor, the other half of Ryu and the founder of the Fou Empire, who went to sleep with a promise that he would take back the throne once he awoke. The current Emperor would rather he didn't. General Yohm hunts him across the country, sets forests on fire and throws monster after monster at him until Fou-Lu crashes into the woods, barely alive.

He wakes up in a little farming village, where a kind woman named Mami takes care of him, and for a while, it's genuinely sweet. Then imperial troops show up, Mami helps him escape, and the Empire fires at him. Before he blacks out, he realises that Mami's life was used to power the weapon. Wanting to wipe out humanity might still be a bit much, but quite frankly, I'd be grumpy too.

Loewe's backstory is incredibly bleak: he grew up in Hamel, a small Erebonian village near the Liberl border, and he was in love with Joshua's older sister, Karin. When the village was massacred to start a war, he lost his family and Karin, and he was right there when it happened. That alone would be enough to send anyone down a dark path.

What really gets me, though, is what happened afterwards: once the war was over, the massacre was quietly covered up, and the official story was that a landslide had destroyed the road to the village. Loewe had no way of seeking justice and nobody to even acknowledge what happened, so he and Joshua made Karin's grave themselves.

So he joined Ouroboros, became its Enforcer No. II, the Sword Emperor, and set out to make the world face the injustices it would rather sweep under the rug. He is cold and terrifyingly strong whenever he shows up, but he still looks out for Joshua for Karin's sake. Without spoiling too much, finding out who was really behind Hamel only makes it worse.

The old school villains really were some of the best, as these SNES JRPGs demonstrate.

I have played Tales of Symphonia more times than I can count, and Mithos gets more tragic with every single playthrough. Long before the game begins, he and his sister Martel were half-elves, hated by humans and elves alike, and driven out of their home because of it. Even so, they went on to end the Ancient Kharlan War together with Kratos and Yuan, and became heroes.

Then Martel was killed, and her dying wish for a world without discrimination turned into something rather sinister in his hands: the Age of Lifeless Beings, where everyone would be the same emotionless being, so that there would be nothing left to discriminate against. Over 4,000 years, that idea only gets worse. By the end, he is mostly fixated on bringing his sister back.

The game clearly wants you to see him as the villain, but it also makes you understand him, and that is what makes him so well written. Raine and Genis have to hide that they're half-elves to protect her teaching job and his education, and even they can't fully dismiss his points. Tales of Symphonia is quite heavy-handed about discrimination, I will say, but it was pretty profound.

Psaro's motivation is almost sweet, as far as wanting to wipe out humanity goes: he is in love with Rose, an elf who cries ruby tears. Naturally, greedy humans want those tears, not knowing that they break very easily, so Psaro builds her a little tower far away from all of them. Rose, meanwhile, keeps asking him to make peace with humans, which he refuses to do.

He isn't innocent, mind you. Egged on by his advisor Aamon, and after hearing that a human hero is prophesied to defeat him, he starts hunting down young humans, which is how the Hero's village gets destroyed at the start of Chapter 5. When Rose is then killed by humans, he loses it completely and transforms himself into Psaro the Manslayer.

The remakes added a sixth chapter, and that is why he made this list. You find a World Tree flower that can bring someone back from the dead, use it on Rose, and her tears turn Psaro back to normal. It also turns out that Aamon arranged her death to take over monsterkind himself, so Psaro joins your party to deal with him. He even got his own game in 2023, Dragon Quest Monsters: The Dark Prince, which feels like a well-earned redemption arc.

Saturos and Menardi were right, and boy, does that annoy me. For the entire first Golden Sun, they are the villains: they raid Mt. Aleph, steal the Elemental Stars and set off to light the four Elemental Lighthouses, which would release Alchemy back into the world. Alchemy was sealed away because it could destroy everything in the wrong hands, so naturally, you chase them across the continent and stop them.

Then The Lost Age hands you Felix, who has been travelling with them all along, and the whole story flips. Without Alchemy, the world of Weyard is slowly dying, and its edges are crumbling into the void. Their hometown of Prox sits right next to the Mars Lighthouse at the far north of the world, and it is drifting closer to that edge by the day. Menardi's younger sister Karst and her partner Agatio carry on where the first two left off, because their entire village depends on it.

Instead of explaining any of that, they went for sneaky and threatening, and they even kept Felix's family locked up in Prox to make sure he'd cooperate. I do understand why, though: nobody was going to believe two strangers claiming that the world was falling apart, especially when hardly anyone could ever travel far enough to see it. A little more communication would have saved everyone a lot of trouble.

#4116. God Of War Sons Of Sparta Gets PS4 Version And New Content Next Monday

It's been about nine months since Sony Santa Monica and Mega Cat Studios dropped God of War Sons of Sparta as a surprise reveal and launch during a State of Play. If you haven't checked it out yet, the developers are giving you some new reasons to today, unveiling two new modes and a new platform: PlayStation 4.

If you don't remember, God of War Sons of Sparta is a prequel spin-off of the God of War series, showing protagonist Kratos as a 13-year-old soldier, long before his god-killing days. The game features 2D combat and a Metroidvania-style map, along with a fully voiced cast of characters including Scott Menville (who you might recognize as Robin in Teen Titans) as Kratos' brother Deimos, Jack Quaid (who will voice a different character in God of War Laufey next year), and TC Carson, who returns from the original trilogy as the voice of adult Kratos.

Announced in a post on the PlayStation Blog today, Sons of Sparta is making the jump back to Sony's previous console, which is now (brace yourself) 13 years old. Sons of Sparta's 2D pixel art is far less demanding than the other God of War entries, though, so it's no surprise this was possible – it's mainly surprising that they're doing it at all.

For PS5 players who already own the game, developer Mega Cat is also adding two new modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode. Hermes Mode, named after the Greek god of wind, mail, and speed, is a speedrun mode that encourages you to beat the game as quickly as possible, complete with a split-based timer in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. Meanwhile, Erebus Mode, named after one of the domains of the underworld (you'll be familiar with it if you've played the Hades games), makes the game far deadlier as Kratos and all his foes die in a single hit. You'll have to wait until you beat the game once to unlock Erebus Mode, but you can access Hermes Mode from a fresh save by entering the following (and semi-familiar) code in the start menu: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, L1, R1, Touchpad.

The free update and PS4 version will be available next Monday, November 16, at midnight local time. For more Sons of Sparta, check out our review. For more God of War, bad news: God of War Laufey was just delayed until May.
